scenarios.title: Morning after a promotion: validate the new DC
scenarios.context: You promoted LAB-DC01 to a domain controller last night. Before users arrive, run the full validation pass a real admin runs: replication, DNS, SYSVOL, and time sync.
objectives: Check time sync (Kerberos breaks past 5 minutes of skew)

tasks.task: Run dcdiag /q and repadmin /replsummary
tasks.guidance: Quiet output is good output. Any error here stops the line — fix before users log on.
tasks.verify: dcdiag silent; repadmin shows 0 fails, largest delta under 60 minutes

tasks.task: Confirm the SYSVOL share and NETLOGON share exist
tasks.guidance: net share | findstr SYSVOL — if missing, run dcdiag /test:netlogons and check the DFSR event log.
tasks.verify: Both shares listed

tasks.task: Check time: w32tm /query /status
tasks.guidance: Stratum should be sane and offset small. Point the DC at a reliable NTP source: w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:"time.windows.com" /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:yes /update.
tasks.verify: Offset under 1 second; source is your configured peer

tasks.task: Create a test user and confirm replication attributes
tasks.guidance: New-ADUser -Name 'replication-test' ... then Get-ADUser replication-test -Server lab-dc01.lab.local — proves ADWS and the directory are serving.
tasks.verify: Test user retrievable immediately

scenarios.title: The printer VLAN can't reach the print server
scenarios.context: Printers live on VLAN 30 (192.168.30.0/24); the print server is on the server segment. Jobs spool but never print. Find the layer at fault.
objectives: Map the path printer -> gateway -> firewall -> server
Test each hop and each required port
Fix the actual fault, not the symptom

tasks.task: From a workstation on VLAN 30, ping the print server
tasks.guidance: If ping fails, it is routing/firewall. If ping works but printing fails, it is ports or the spooler.
tasks.verify: Ping result recorded either way

tasks.task: Test-NetConnection print-srv -Port 445 and -Port 9100
tasks.guidance: 445 = SMB (driver/share access), 9100 = raw printing. Note which passes.
tasks.verify: Port test results for both ports recorded

tasks.task: Check the pfSense rule between VLAN 30 and the server segment
tasks.guidance: Firewall > Rules > VLAN30: you need pass rules for TCP 445, 139, 9100, 515 from the printer subnet to the print server IP.
tasks.verify: Rules present and logged as passing (check the firewall log)

tasks.task: Confirm the printer's gateway and DNS
tasks.guidance: Printers with wrong gateways are a classic: print the config page and verify gateway = the VLAN 30 interface.
tasks.verify: Printer config page shows correct gateway

scenarios.title: Alert storm: 40 hosts report 'unreachable' at once
scenarios.context: Zabbix fires 40 host-down alerts within two minutes at 9:04 AM. Forty hosts do not die at once — something shared broke. Triage like an on-call engineer.
objectives: Resist the urge to touch hosts; find the common dependency
Resolve and tune the alert so it doesn't page 40 times next time

tasks.task: List the 40 hosts: do they share a switch, a hypervisor host, or a network segment?
tasks.guidance: Monitoring > Problems > filter by time; export the host list and compare subnets. Shared fate = shared cause.
tasks.verify: Common factor identified (e.g. all on Hyper-V host HV-02, or all behind switch SW-3)

tasks.task: Check the infrastructure ABOVE the hosts: hypervisor host status, switch uplinks, the Zabbix proxy if one is in path
tasks.guidance: One ping to the hypervisor host tells you more than 40 host checks.
tasks.verify: Root device identified (e.g. HV-02 unreachable)

tasks.task: Fix the root (reboot hung host, reseat uplink, etc.) and watch recovery cascade
tasks.guidance: Fix one thing, watch the Problems dashboard clear top-down.
tasks.verify: All 40 clear without per-host intervention

tasks.task: Add dependency-aware alerting so next time you get ONE alert
tasks.guidance: Zabbix: set the hypervisor/switch as the hosts' 'proxy' parent or use trigger dependencies — child alerts suppressed when the parent is down.
tasks.verify: Dependency configured; document it in the runbook

scenarios.title: Restore the finance share from last night's backup
scenarios.context: Finance deleted the Q3 folder from \\lab-fs01\departments at 10 AM. The nightly backup ran at 2 AM. Restore it — and prove nothing else changed.
objectives: Restore to an alternate location first (never overwrite live data blindly)
Verify integrity, then put it back

tasks.task: wbadmin get versions — pick last night's 02:00 version identifier
tasks.guidance: Match the version timestamp to before the 10 AM deletion.
tasks.verify: Version identifier copied

tasks.task: Recover to C:\RestoreStaging: wbadmin start recovery -version:<id> -itemType:File -items:D:\Shares\Departments\Finance\Q3 -recoveryTarget:C:\RestoreStaging -quiet
tasks.guidance: Alternate location first — if the backup is corrupt you haven't touched the live share.
tasks.verify: Q3 folder present under C:\RestoreStaging

tasks.task: Verify: count files, spot-open the largest spreadsheet, compare against the finance lead's expectation
tasks.guidance: A restore you don't verify is a rumor. Check counts and open the critical files.
tasks.verify: File count matches; spot checks open cleanly

tasks.task: Copy back to the live share with robocopy /MIR from staging, preserving timestamps
tasks.guidance: robocopy C:\RestoreStaging\Q3 D:\Shares\Departments\Finance\Q3 /MIR /COPY:DAT — then confirm NTFS permissions inherited correctly.
tasks.verify: Live share restored; permissions correct; user confirms

scenarios.title: lab-linux01 won't take SSH after a reboot
scenarios.context: The Ubuntu box rebooted overnight for updates. Now SSH times out. The services depend on it. Work the console-first recovery flow.
objectives: Get in via the hypervisor console
Determine whether it's network, SSH daemon, or firewall
Fix and add a guard so it doesn't recur silently

tasks.task: Open the hypervisor console and log in locally
tasks.guidance: When SSH is dead, the console is your crash cart. Confirm the OS actually booted.
tasks.verify: Local login works; uptime shows recent boot

tasks.task: systemctl status ssh; ss -tlnp | grep :22
tasks.guidance: Is sshd running AND listening? Distinguish 'dead daemon' from 'blocked port'.
tasks.verify: sshd state and listener status recorded

tasks.task: ip addr; ip route; ping 192.168.10.1
tasks.guidance: No IP = netplan/DHCP issue; IP but no gateway ping = vSwitch/VLAN issue.
tasks.verify: Network layer verdict recorded

tasks.task: Fix the found cause (e.g. netplan yaml broken by update: fix indentation, netplan apply; or ufw re-enabled with wrong rules)
tasks.guidance: Fix one layer, re-test SSH from your workstation after each change.
tasks.verify: SSH works from workstation

tasks.task: Add a Zabbix agent check on TCP 22 and an 'unreachable' trigger
tasks.guidance: You should have been paged before the ticket. Close that gap now.
tasks.verify: Trigger exists and is tested

scenarios.title: New-hire onboarding day (the full loop)
scenarios.context: It's Monday 8 AM. Three new hires start in the IT department. Run the complete onboarding loop: account, hardware, access, orientation — and document everything for the audit trail.
objectives: Leave a paper trail the auditors will love

tasks.task: Create the three AD accounts in OU=Users with the bulk script (IL27-TERM-01 pattern), temp passwords, change-at-logon
tasks.guidance: Script it — Monday-morning clicking is how typos become security incidents.
tasks.verify: 3 accounts exist, enabled, in correct OU, password-change flagged

tasks.task: Add to groups: LAB-IT for all three; no Domain Admins, no exceptions — document any extra access as a ticket
tasks.guidance: Least privilege on day one. Elevated access goes through the access-request process, not onboarding.
tasks.verify: Group memberships match the access matrix; ticket numbers recorded

tasks.task: Image or configure laptops: join to lab.local, confirm GPOs apply (gpresult), verify Defender + BitLocker status
tasks.guidance: A laptop that skipped the baseline GPO is a rogue device with a welcome mat.
tasks.verify: gpresult shows baseline GPOs; BitLocker encrypting; Defender real-time on

tasks.task: Orientation checklist: acceptable-use policy signed, phishing briefing done, MFA enrolled, manager intro
tasks.guidance: The human controls matter as much as the technical ones — log each with date/time.
tasks.verify: Signed checklist filed per hire

tasks.task: Offboarding rehearsal: disable (don't delete) one test account and confirm its access dies
tasks.guidance: Disable-ADAccount testuser; verify login fails and group memberships remain for audit. Deletion destroys the audit trail — disable first, delete per retention policy.
tasks.verify: Test account cannot authenticate; audit log shows the disable event

dc_down.text: Monday 7:55 AM. LAB-DC01 won't boot — it hangs at the Windows logo with spinning dots. Users arrive in 5 minutes and nothing authenticates without the DC. What's your FIRST move?

choices.label: Boot into Directory Services Restore Mode and seize roles
choices.feedback: Too drastic for step one — you don't even know what's wrong yet, and seizing roles on a sick DC can corrupt AD.

choices.label: Check the hypervisor console for the actual error / boot into Safe Mode to observe
choices.feedback: Correct instinct: diagnose before you treat. The console often shows the real error (disk, update, driver).

choices.label: Restore the whole VM from last night's backup immediately
choices.feedback: Restore is a valid card, but playing it before a 2-minute diagnosis wastes your fastest recovery path if it's something trivial.

choices.label: Tell users to work offline until IT figures it out
choices.feedback: Giving up before diagnosing is never the first move — and cached credentials only go so far.

observe.text: Safe Mode shows: 'We couldn't complete the updates. Undoing changes.' A Windows Update wedged the boot. Users are arriving. Now what?

choices.label: Let it finish undoing changes — monitor, and prep the backup restore in parallel
choices.feedback: Right call: the undo usually completes in 10-20 minutes. Prepping the restore in parallel means you're covered either way.

choices.label: Hard-power-off the VM mid-undo to speed things up
choices.feedback: Never interrupt 'undoing changes' — you'll convert a slow boot into a corrupted component store.

choices.label: Boot DSRM and restore System State from backup
choices.feedback: Premature: DSRM restore is for AD corruption, not a wedged update. Let the rollback finish first.

patient.text: The undo finished — LAB-DC01 booted cleanly at 8:20. dcdiag is clean. What's the correct follow-through?

choices.label: Document the incident, pause automatic updates on DCs, schedule updates in a maintenance window
choices.feedback: Correct: DCs get updates on YOUR schedule with a tested rollback plan, never auto-install at 3 AM before a workday.

choices.label: Do nothing — it's working now
choices.feedback: The same update will wedge it again next cycle. 'Working now' without a preventive change is just scheduling the next outage.

choices.label: Reinstall the server from scratch to be safe
choices.feedback: The system is healthy and dcdiag is clean — a rebuild burns hours for zero gain and risks new mistakes.

patient.explanation: Correct path: observe first (Safe Mode diagnosis), let the update rollback complete while prepping restore in parallel, then prevent recurrence with a DC maintenance-window policy. The discipline is: diagnose, protect your options, fix, then make it not happen again.

dsrm_panic.text: You seized roles in DSRM on a DC whose database may be fine. Replication partners now see conflicting role holders. What did this cost you?

choices.label: A metadata cleanup and possible USN rollback risk — seizing without diagnosing was the error
choices.feedback: Exactly. Role seizure is for a DEAD DC, not a sick one. Now you own a cleanup.

dsrm_panic.explanation: Role seizure is a last resort for a permanently dead DC. Doing it on a recoverable DC creates more damage than the original fault.

restore_now.text: The restore is running — 45 minutes. Meanwhile a colleague checks the console: it was just 'undoing changes' and would have finished in 15 minutes. Lesson?

choices.label: Diagnose for 2 minutes before committing to the 45-minute path
choices.feedback: Right. The restore wasn't wrong, just premature — a 2-minute console check would have picked the faster path.

restore_now.explanation: Restores are powerful but slow. A quick diagnosis first lets you choose the fastest correct recovery.

give_up.text: By 9:30 users can't reach file shares (Kerberos needs the DC) and you're still 'figuring it out.' What should step one have been?

choices.label: Console diagnosis — the 2-minute check that drives every later decision
choices.feedback: Yes. Every incident starts with facts, not announcements.

give_up.explanation: Communicate status AND diagnose in parallel — but never substitute announcements for diagnosis.

powerkill.text: The VM now blue-screens with INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE. The component store is corrupted. Your options narrowed to one:

choices.label: Restore from last night's backup (the path you should have prepped, not interrupted)
choices.feedback: Correct — and now it's the ONLY path, plus you lost the 15-minute natural recovery.

powerkill.explanation: Interrupting a Windows rollback corrupts the component store. Patience during 'undoing changes' is a technical requirement, not a virtue.

dsrm_restore.text: DSRM System State restore on a merely update-wedged DC: it works, but took 90 minutes and forced a non-authoritative dance. The faster path was:

choices.label: Letting the rollback finish (~15 min) — match the tool to the diagnosis
choices.feedback: Right tool, wrong incident. Diagnosis drives tool selection.

dsrm_restore.explanation: System State restore is for AD corruption. A wedged update just needs its rollback to complete.

done_right.text: Incident closed: 25-minute outage, root cause documented, DCs moved to a Sunday 2 AM maintenance window with snapshots. The review board asks what you'll do differently. Answer:

choices.label: Nothing about the response — but updates now go to a canary member server first, then DCs
choices.feedback: Mature answer: the response was sound; you're adding a canary tier so DCs never take an untested update.

done_right.explanation: Correct-path explanation: diagnose (console/Safe Mode) → protect options (prep restore in parallel) → let the safe path play out → prevent recurrence (maintenance windows + canary tier). Total: 25 minutes, one lesson institutionalized.

done_wrong.text: Three weeks later the same update wedges the DC again — this time during payroll processing. The post-mortem writes itself.

choices.label: Restart the scenario with the maintenance-window lesson applied
choices.feedback: Good — run it again and pick the preventive path this time.

done_wrong.explanation: Unfixed root causes recur at the worst possible time. The follow-through IS the fix.

overkill.text: Six hours into a rebuild, you realize the original system was healthy. The business lost a day for nothing.

choices.label: Restart and trust the diagnostics when they're clean
choices.feedback: dcdiag clean + successful boot = healthy. Don't rebuild healthy systems.

overkill.explanation: Rebuilding a verified-healthy system is the most expensive form of anxiety.

lesson.text: Lesson logged. The core discipline this scenario teaches:

choices.label: Return to start and run the correct path
choices.feedback: Diagnose first, protect options, match the tool to the fault, then prevent recurrence.

lesson.explanation: Diagnose → options → correct tool → prevention. That's the whole incident-response loop in one scenario.

end.text: Scenario complete. You handled a down DC in 25 minutes and left the environment better than you found it. That's the job.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Loop back and try a different first move to see the consequences.

end.explanation: Mastery = correct path under time pressure, plus institutional learning.

branchingScenarios.title: DNS is down for the whole office

dns_down.text: 9:12 AM: tickets flood in — 'internet is down,' 'can't reach anything.' You test: ping 8.8.8.8 works, but no name resolves anywhere. DNS is down office-wide. First action?

choices.label: Check whether the DNS Server service is running on LAB-DC01
choices.feedback: Yes — start with the service that owns the symptom. One command, thirty seconds.

choices.label: Reboot LAB-DC01 immediately
choices.feedback: Rebooting the DC is the nuclear option as step one — it kills auth for everyone and you still won't know the cause.

choices.label: Tell users to use 8.8.8.8 as a workaround
choices.feedback: That bypasses internal DNS entirely — lab.local stops resolving and AD breaks. Workarounds must not break identity.

choices.label: Assume the ISP is down and call them
choices.feedback: Ping 8.8.8.8 works — the ISP is fine. The evidence already rules this out; read it.

check_service.text: Get-Service DNS on LAB-DC01: Status = Stopped. It stopped at 9:04 AM. What next?

choices.label: Start the service, then immediately check WHY it stopped (event log)
choices.feedback: Correct: restore service first (users are down), then find the cause before it recurs.

choices.label: Start the service and walk away
choices.feedback: Service is up — but if you don't learn why it stopped, you'll be back here tomorrow.

choices.label: Set it to Automatic and reboot the server
choices.feedback: It was already Automatic — that's why it tried to start at boot. The setting isn't the problem.

start_and_why.text: DNS is running again — tickets stop. Event log shows: Event 769, 'The DNS server is out of memory' — wait, no: Event 150, 'could not open socket for 192.168.20.10.' Something else grabbed port 53. Suspects?

choices.label: Check for a second DNS/DHCP service or a container bound to port 53
choices.feedback: Right instinct: port conflicts are the #1 'DNS just stopped' cause on lab servers.

choices.label: Add more RAM to the DC
choices.feedback: Event 150 is a socket bind failure, not memory pressure. Treat the actual error, not a guess.

choices.label: Reinstall the DNS role
choices.feedback: The role is fine — something is squatting on its port. Reinstalling changes nothing.

port_conflict.text: netstat -ano | findstr :53 shows PID 2144 listening on 0.0.0.0:53. Tasklist: it's a Docker proxy from a Pi-hole test container someone left running on the DC. Resolution?

choices.label: Stop/remove the rogue container, restart DNS, document 'no test containers on DCs' as policy
choices.feedback: Correct: remove the squatter, restore the service, and make the rule explicit so it sticks.

choices.label: Just kill the PID
choices.feedback: The container restarts on reboot (restart policy) — killing the process is whack-a-mole.

choices.label: Move DNS to a different port
choices.feedback: DNS must be on 53 — every client on earth expects it there. Move the squatter, never the service.

port_conflict.explanation: Correct path: verify the service → restore it → read the actual event → find the port squatter → remove it permanently → policy. Total downtime ~10 minutes, and the 'no test workloads on DCs' rule prevents the sequel.

start_only.text: Next morning, 9:04 AM again: DNS stopped again. The squatter container restarted with the DC. Now you do the full job:

choices.label: Remove the container and write the policy
choices.feedback: Now you've paid the tuition — make the lesson permanent.

start_only.explanation: Uninvestigated root causes recur on a schedule. The second outage is the one you chose.

reboot_dc.text: The DC reboots — 8 minutes of zero authentication, file shares drop, and DNS is STILL stopped because the squatter container auto-started again. What did the reboot buy?

choices.label: Nothing but an 8-minute full outage — diagnose before rebooting
choices.feedback: Reboots feel decisive and teach you nothing. Check the service first.

reboot_dc.explanation: Rebooting without diagnosis converts a 2-minute fix into an 8-minute outage and leaves the cause running.

workaround.text: Users set 8.8.8.8 manually. Now group policy fails, file shares prompt for passwords, and 'lab.local' doesn't resolve. The helpdesk queue doubled. Revert and:

choices.label: Go back and check the DNS service properly
choices.feedback: Workarounds that break identity are worse than the outage.

workaround.explanation: External DNS as a workaround breaks AD. Never bypass internal DNS on domain members.

blame_isp.text: ISP support: 'our network is fine, and your pings prove it.' Twenty minutes lost. The evidence (ping works, names fail) always pointed at:

choices.label: Local DNS — back to the DC and check the service
choices.feedback: Read the evidence: IP works + names fail = DNS, and it's YOUR DNS.

blame_isp.explanation: IP-reachable but name-unresolvable is never the ISP. It's your resolver chain.

more_ram.text: You added RAM. DNS still can't bind port 53. The event log still says socket failure. Treat the:

choices.label: Actual error: find what's on port 53
choices.feedback: Always treat the logged error, not the guessed cause.

more_ram.explanation: Event 150 names the problem: something holds the socket. Find it.

reinstall.text: After a 30-minute role reinstall, DNS starts — then stops again at the next reboot when the container returns. The role was never broken:

choices.label: Find the port squatter instead
choices.feedback: Reinstalling a healthy role to fix a port conflict is surgery for a splinter.

reinstall.explanation: If a reinstall 'fixes' it temporarily, the cause is environmental, not the role.

kill_pid.text: PID killed — DNS starts. After the next reboot, the container (restart: always) grabs port 53 again. Permanent fix:

choices.label: Remove the container / its restart policy
choices.feedback: Processes come back; configurations persist. Fix the configuration.

kill_pid.explanation: Kill the process AND its resurrection mechanism.

move_port.text: You moved DNS to 5353. Zero clients can resolve anything — DNS on a nonstandard port might as well not exist. Undo and:

choices.label: Remove the squatter; DNS stays on 53
choices.feedback: Infrastructure services live on their standard ports. Full stop.

move_port.explanation: Standard ports are a contract with every client. Never move the service; move the squatter.

done_right.text: DNS stable for a week. Your runbook now has: 'DNS down → Get-Service DNS → event log → netstat :53 → no test workloads on DCs.' The review board is happy. Close it:

choices.label: Close the incident with the runbook update attached
choices.feedback: An incident isn't closed when service restores — it's closed when the runbook learns.

done_right.explanation: Correct-path explanation: service check → restore → actual error → port squatter → permanent removal → policy + runbook. Ten minutes of downtime, zero recurrences.

auto_reboot.text: It WAS already Automatic — the service tried and failed to start because port 53 is taken. The setting was never the problem. Check:

choices.label: What's actually on port 53
choices.feedback: Settings don't fix conflicts. Evidence does.

auto_reboot.explanation: Verify assumptions: 'Automatic' doesn't help when the port is occupied.

end.text: Scenario complete. Office-wide DNS outage resolved in ~10 minutes with a runbook update. That's infrastructure work.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Try the wrong first moves to feel their cost.

end.explanation: Mastery = fastest correct path + the recurrence prevention.

ransom_alert.text: 2:14 PM: Zabbix fires — LAB-W11-01 is renaming hundreds of files per minute, and a ransom note appeared on the desktop. This is the real thing (or the drill — treat it as real). FIRST action?

choices.label: Isolate the host from the network immediately (disable NIC / firewall-block its IP)
choices.feedback: Correct: containment first. Every second online is more encrypted files and possible lateral movement.

choices.label: Start deleting the encrypted files to clean up
choices.feedback: Deleting destroys evidence AND the only copies you might recover. Never delete during containment.

choices.label: Pay the ransom to get the data back fast
choices.feedback: No — payment funds crime, often doesn't deliver a working key, and in the drill it's disallowed. Recovery comes from backups.

choices.label: Shut the host down hard right now
choices.feedback: Tempting, but a hard shutdown loses RAM forensics and can corrupt the evidence snapshot. Isolate first, snapshot, then decide.

isolate.text: Host isolated — NIC disabled at the hypervisor. File renaming stopped. Next, in order?

choices.label: Snapshot the VM for evidence, then identify patient zero (how did it get in?)
choices.feedback: Right: preserve evidence BEFORE remediation. Snapshots are cheap; lost forensics are gone forever.

choices.label: Immediately restore from backup
choices.feedback: Restore without knowing the entry point = reinfection. Find patient zero first.

choices.label: Re-enable the NIC briefly to 'check something'
choices.feedback: Reconnecting an infected host, even briefly, risks lateral movement. The one exception is a controlled forensic VLAN — not the production LAN.

evidence.text: Snapshot taken. PowerShell history shows a malicious macro-enabled attachment opened at 1:58 PM; a scheduled task 'Updater' runs the payload hourly. Eradication plan?

choices.label: Delete the scheduled task, remove the payload + persistence, kill related processes — then verify no other persistence (registry Run keys, WMI)
choices.feedback: Correct and complete: kill ALL persistence mechanisms, not just the obvious one.

choices.label: Just delete the ransom note
choices.feedback: The note is a symptom. The scheduled task will re-encrypt everything within the hour.

choices.label: Run a full antivirus scan and call it done
choices.feedback: AV helps, but the scheduled task + registry persistence need manual removal and verification.

eradicate.text: Persistence removed, processes dead, second scan clean. The user's Documents are encrypted (.locked). Recovery?

choices.label: Restore from last night's backup to an alternate location, verify, then return to the user — and check backup integrity for the whole share
choices.feedback: Correct: alternate-location restore, verify before touching live data, and confirm the backups themselves aren't compromised.

choices.label: Try a free decryptor from the internet on the production files
choices.feedback: Decryptors work only for specific families and can corrupt files further. Verify the family first, test on COPIES.

choices.label: Tell the user the files are gone
choices.feedback: Not until you've checked the backups — that's literally what they're for.

eradicate.explanation: Correct path: isolate → snapshot/evidence → find entry point → eradicate ALL persistence → restore from verified backup → lessons learned. Speed matters, but order matters more.

delete_files.text: You deleted encrypted files — including the ransom note with the incident ID and the originals you could have restored over. Forensics is now guesswork.

choices.label: Restart: isolate first, touch nothing
choices.feedback: Containment before cleanup. Always.

delete_files.explanation: During containment, every file is evidence. Deletion is a post-recovery, approved action.

pay.text: Payment sent. No key arrived — and the incident is now a legal/compliance event too. The correct recovery was always:

choices.label: Isolate and restore from backup — restart the scenario
choices.feedback: Backups are the ransom you pay in advance, on your terms.

pay.explanation: Paying doesn't work reliably and creates new liability. Tested backups are the answer.

poweroff.text: Hard shutdown done. RAM forensics lost; the disk snapshot may be crash-inconsistent. It works, but you paid a forensics tax. Better first move was:

choices.label: Network isolation (keeps the host alive for forensics)
choices.feedback: Isolation stops the bleeding without killing the patient.

poweroff.explanation: Isolate > power off: same containment, preserved forensics.

restore_fast.text: Restored from backup — and the scheduled task you never found re-encrypted everything by 4 PM. The step you skipped:

choices.label: Patient-zero + persistence removal BEFORE restore
choices.feedback: Eradicate, then restore. Order is everything.

restore_fast.explanation: Restoring onto a still-compromised host is just scheduling the second incident.

reconnect.text: During the 90 seconds online, the payload scanned the subnet and hit the file server's SMB. You now have TWO incidents. The rule:

choices.label: Isolated means isolated — restart
choices.feedback: Never reconnect an infected host to production. Ever.

reconnect.explanation: One reconnection can double your incident. Containment is binary.

note_only.text: One hour later the scheduled task fired and re-encrypted the restored files. You treated the symptom. Treat the:

choices.label: Persistence mechanisms — all of them
choices.feedback: Find every autorun, task, service, and WMI consumer.

note_only.explanation: Ransomware is a persistence problem wearing an encryption costume.

av_only.text: AV removed the payload binary but the scheduled task now fails loudly every hour and the registry Run key re-downloads it. Manual eradication was still required:

choices.label: Back up and do the full persistence sweep
choices.feedback: AV is a layer, not the whole eradication.

av_only.explanation: Verify eradication; don't assume the scanner found every persistence trick.

decryptor.text: The decryptor was for a different family — it corrupted the headers of 200 files. Test decryptors on COPIES, and only after identifying the family. The reliable path:

choices.label: Verified backup restore
choices.feedback: Backups don't care which ransomware family it is.

giveup_data.text: The user mentions the 2 AM backup — which you never checked. The data was recoverable the whole time. Always:

choices.label: Check backups before declaring data lost
choices.feedback: The backup exists precisely for this sentence.

giveup_data.explanation: 'Files are gone' is a verdict you earn only after the backup check.

restore.text: Files restored and verified; user working again by 5 PM. Last step — the one that makes the next incident cheaper:

choices.label: Write the incident report: timeline, entry point (phishing macro), dwell time, and add controls — attachment sandboxing, AppLocker, backup immutability
choices.feedback: The report converts an incident into institutional immunity.

restore.explanation: Correct-path explanation: isolate → evidence → entry point → full eradication → verified restore → incident report with new controls. The report is what makes this the LAST time this vector works.

end.text: Scenario complete. You ran a full IR lifecycle: 3-hour turnaround, data recovered, controls added. That's the drill the interview will ask about.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Try skipping the evidence step and feel the cost.

end.explanation: Mastery = containment discipline + evidence hygiene + verified recovery + institutional learning.

vpn_down.text: 8:02 AM: the branch office calls — they can't reach anything at HQ. The site-to-site VPN tunnel on pfSense shows DOWN. Your first diagnostic?

choices.label: Check whether it's the tunnel or the underlying internet on either side (ping each WAN, check gateway status)
choices.feedback: Correct: VPNs die when the underlay dies. Rule out internet/path issues before touching crypto config.

choices.label: Delete and rebuild the VPN tunnel from scratch
choices.feedback: Rebuilding a tunnel whose config was fine yesterday wastes an hour and risks new typos. Diagnose first.

choices.label: Reboot both firewalls
choices.feedback: Rebooting firewalls drops ALL traffic at both sites for minutes — as step one it's pure hope.

choices.label: Assume the branch ISP is down and wait
choices.feedback: Assumption without a single test. One ping disproves or confirms it in seconds.

underlay.text: Both WANs are up; gateways respond; each firewall reaches the internet. The underlay is fine — the tunnel itself won't establish. Next?

choices.label: Check the IPsec logs on both sides for phase 1 / phase 2 errors
choices.feedback: Right: the logs name the failing phase. Phase 1 = authentication/peer; phase 2 = selectors/proposals.

choices.label: Change the pre-shared key on both sides
choices.feedback: If the key were wrong it would never have worked — it worked yesterday. Don't churn what isn't broken.

choices.label: Switch from IKEv2 to IKEv1 to 'simplify'
choices.feedback: Downgrading crypto to dodge a config issue weakens security for zero diagnostic gain.

logs.text: HQ log: 'no matching proposal found' during phase 2. Branch recently updated their firewall firmware last night. Diagnosis?

choices.label: The firmware update reset/changed the phase 2 proposals — compare both sides' encryption/hash/DH settings and align them
choices.feedback: Correct: 'no matching proposal' after a firmware update = the update changed defaults. Align the crypto maps.

choices.label: The tunnel is being attacked — block the branch IP
choices.feedback: It's your own branch office failing negotiation, not an attacker. Read the log literally.

choices.label: Increase the tunnel MTU
choices.feedback: MTU issues cause black-holed traffic AFTER establishment, not proposal failures during negotiation.

logs.explanation: Correct path: verify underlay → read IPsec logs → identify the phase → align proposals after the firmware change. Most 'tunnel down' incidents are config drift, not crypto failure.

align.text: Proposals aligned (AES-256/GCM, SHA256, DH14 both sides) — tunnel is UP, branch traffic flowing. Prevent the sequel:

choices.label: Document the exact crypto settings in the runbook and add a firmware-update checklist item: 'verify VPN proposals post-update'
choices.feedback: Config drift is the enemy; the runbook is the weapon. The checklist item costs nothing and prevents the repeat.

align.explanation: Correct-path explanation: underlay check → log-driven phase identification → proposal alignment after firmware drift → runbook + checklist. Thirty minutes, one permanent checklist item.

rebuild.text: An hour into the rebuild you find a typo in the new PSK — and the original tunnel config (which was fine) is gone. Meanwhile the branch is still down. The lesson:

choices.label: Export/backup firewall configs before touching them; diagnose first
choices.feedback: Rebuilds without backups turn one problem into two.

rebuild.explanation: Never rebuild crypto config without a backup of the working version.

reboot_fw.text: Both firewalls rebooted: 6 minutes of total outage at both sites, tunnel still down (it was a proposal mismatch). Reboots don't fix:

choices.label: Configuration drift — back to the logs
choices.feedback: Reboots fix stuck processes, not mismatched settings.

reboot_fw.explanation: If it worked yesterday and nothing rebooted it into failure, the cause is config or peer-side change.

wait.text: Two hours later the branch manager calls your boss. A 30-second ping test at 8:03 would have shown the underlay was fine. Never:

choices.label: Substitute waiting for testing — restart with the underlay check
choices.feedback: Hope is not a diagnostic step.

wait.explanation: Every minute of assumption is a minute the business is down.

psk.text: New PSK on both sides — tunnel still down, and now you've introduced a change to chase. The log said 'no matching proposal' — that's phase 2 selectors, not authentication. Read the:

choices.label: Logs literally, then align proposals
choices.feedback: The log told you the answer. Trust it.

psk.explanation: Match the fix to the logged error, not to a hunch.

downgrade.text: IKEv1 'worked' — by weakening the negotiation. Security review flags it next week and you redo the whole thing properly. The right fix was always:

choices.label: Aligning the IKEv2 proposals
choices.feedback: Never trade security for convenience in a diagnostic shortcut.

downgrade.explanation: Downgrading crypto to avoid diagnosis creates a finding you'll have to remediate anyway.

attack.text: You blocked your own branch office IP. Now even the fixed tunnel can't reach HQ. Unblock it and read logs as written:

choices.label: It's a proposal mismatch with your own peer — restart
choices.feedback: Know your peers before you block them.

attack.explanation: Blocking first and reading later turns incidents into self-inflicted outages.

mtu.text: MTU changes did nothing — the tunnel never got past phase 2. MTU matters after establishment. Go back to the:

choices.label: Phase 2 proposal alignment
choices.feedback: Fix the phase that's actually failing.

mtu.explanation: Diagnose the failing phase; fix that phase.

end.text: Scenario complete. Branch back online in ~30 minutes with a runbook update. VPN incidents are config-drift incidents wearing a crypto costume.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Try the rebuild-first path and feel the hour evaporate.

end.explanation: Mastery = underlay first, logs over hunches, align don't rebuild, checklist the drift.

branchingScenarios.title: File server out of disk at 2 AM

disk_full.text: 2:07 AM: your phone buzzes — Zabbix: 'LAB-FS01 D: 98% full.' The file server's data volume is nearly full. Shares will freeze when it hits 100%. First move?

choices.label: Check what's consuming the space before deleting anything
choices.feedback: Correct: at 2 AM, deleting blind risks destroying the wrong data. Assess first — it takes minutes.

choices.label: Delete the biggest files immediately to buy headroom
choices.feedback: The biggest files might be the finance share. 'Biggest first' without identification is how you delete the business.

choices.label: Extend the virtual disk right now
choices.feedback: Extending buys space but if a runaway process is writing (logs, loop), you'll fill the new space too — and you haven't found the cause.

choices.label: Ignore it until morning
choices.feedback: At 98% with active writes, morning might be 100% with frozen shares and a crashed backup. 2 AM pages exist for this.

assess.text: D:\Shares is 380 GB of 400 GB. Breakdown: Departments 180 GB (normal), plus D:\Shares\Temp\video-renders at 190 GB — someone's been dumping 4K video renders to the share for weeks. Action?

choices.label: Confirm with the owner, move renders to proper storage (or quota them), compress/clean temp, then set quotas + alerting
choices.feedback: Correct: the data isn't yours to delete unilaterally — confirm, relocate, then prevent with quotas and earlier alerts.

choices.label: Delete the video-renders folder now
choices.feedback: It's 2 AM and you haven't confirmed what it is. If it's the marketing team's active project, you just became the incident.

choices.label: Just extend the disk to 800 GB and go back to sleep
choices.feedback: You'll be paged again in six weeks with the same folder at 700 GB. Extension without policy is a snooze button.

fix_right.text: Owner confirms: renders are done, safe to archive. You move 190 GB to the archive NAS, D: drops to 48%. Now make 2 AM pages rarer:

choices.label: Set FSRM quotas on the shares (e.g. Temp capped at 50 GB), Zabbix trigger at 80% warning / 90% high, and a monthly storage review
choices.feedback: The full fix: immediate relief + technical prevention (quotas) + earlier alerting + process (review).

choices.label: Nothing — it's fixed
choices.feedback: Without quotas and earlier alerts, this exact page recurs. 'Fixed' without prevention is temporary.

fix_right.explanation: Correct path: assess before acting → identify the real consumer → confirm ownership → relocate → quotas + tiered alerting + review cadence. The 2 AM page becomes a 10 AM warning next time.

delete_big.text: You deleted the 190 GB — it WAS the marketing team's active project, mid-campaign. Restore from backup took 3 hours and the CMO knows your name. Next time:

choices.label: Assess and confirm ownership before deleting anything
choices.feedback: Data has owners. Deletion is a confirmed, approved act.

delete_big.explanation: Never delete unilaterally at 2 AM. Identify, confirm, then act.

extend.text: Disk extended to 800 GB. The render-dumping continues — you're paged again in 5 weeks at 98% of 800 GB, and the backup window no longer fits. The missing piece was:

choices.label: Finding the consumer and setting quotas
choices.feedback: Capacity without policy is just a bigger cliff.

extend.explanation: Extension treats the symptom. Quotas treat the behavior.

ignore.text: 6:30 AM: D: hit 100%. Shares froze mid-save, the backup failed, and three users lost work. The page at 2 AM was the cheap version of this incident:

choices.label: Respond to disk pages promptly — restart the scenario
choices.feedback: 98% at 2 AM never gets better by morning.

ignore.explanation: Disk-full pages are time bombs with visible timers. Defuse them.

delete_renders.text: Deleted at 2 AM, no confirmation. It was active project data. The restore worked, but trust didn't. The rule:

choices.label: Confirm ownership — data deletion needs a name attached
choices.feedback: 'Probably safe' is not an authorization.

delete_renders.explanation: If you can't name the owner who approved deletion, don't delete.

extend_sleep.text: Six weeks later: paged again, 98% of 800 GB, backup window blown. The snooze button worked exactly once. Permanent fix:

choices.label: Quotas + 80% early warning + ownership
choices.feedback: Policy beats capacity, every time.

extend_sleep.explanation: Every extension without policy just reschedules the page.

nothing.text: Four months later the renders are back and so is the page. Prevention is part of the fix:

choices.label: Add the quotas and alerts now
choices.feedback: An incident without prevention is a rehearsal.

nothing.explanation: Close the loop or repeat the incident.

end.text: Scenario complete. A 2 AM page handled with discipline: assessed, confirmed, relocated, quota'd, alerted earlier. The next one pages at 80% during business hours.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Try deleting first and meet the CMO.

end.explanation: Mastery = assess → confirm → relieve → prevent (quotas + tiered alerts + review).

onboard.text: Monday 8 AM: three new IT hires start. Your onboarding checklist is ready. Where do you begin?

choices.label: Create the AD accounts first (identity before everything)
choices.feedback: Correct: every other step — groups, mailbox, laptop login — depends on the identity existing.

choices.label: Hand them laptops first so they can 'get settled'
choices.feedback: Laptops without accounts are expensive paperweights — they can't log in, and you'll redo the setup.

choices.label: Start with the HR paperwork and security briefing
choices.feedback: Important, but the accounts take provisioning time — start the technical chain first, do paperwork in parallel.

choices.label: Give them all Domain Admin 'temporarily' to avoid access tickets
choices.feedback: Never. 'Temporary' Domain Admin is how breaches start. Least privilege from minute one.

identity.text: Accounts created in OU=Users via script, temp passwords set, change-at-logon flagged. Next: access. The hires need file shares, the ticketing system, and VPN. How?

choices.label: Add to role groups (LAB-IT etc.) per the access matrix; file/ticket/VPN access flows from group membership; elevated needs go through access-request tickets
choices.feedback: Correct: role-based access, documented, no standing privilege. This is the answer the interview wants to hear.

choices.label: Clone the access of a senior admin 'to be safe'
choices.feedback: Cloning accumulates privilege nobody reviews — it's how 'temporary' access becomes permanent.

choices.label: Ask each hire what they think they need and grant it
choices.feedback: New hires don't know the access model on day one — that's YOUR job, via the matrix.

least_priv.text: Access provisioned via groups. Laptops: joined to lab.local, baseline GPOs applied (gpresult confirms), Defender on, BitLocker encrypting. Now the human layer:

choices.label: Acceptable-use signature, phishing briefing, MFA enrollment — logged per hire with date/time
choices.feedback: Correct: the technical controls are half the onboarding; the human controls are the other half, and auditors check both.

choices.label: Skip the briefing — they're IT, they know security
choices.feedback: 'They're IT' is how IT gets phished. Everyone gets the briefing; it's also your audit evidence.

choices.label: Do the briefing 'later this week' when things calm down
choices.feedback: Later never comes, and the highest-risk window is the first 72 hours with fresh credentials.

human_layer.text: All three hires are productive by lunch: accounts, access, hardened laptops, briefings logged. One last onboarding discipline — the offboarding rehearsal:

choices.label: Create a test account, disable (not delete) it, verify auth fails and the audit log records it — proving your offboarding actually works
choices.feedback: Elite move: most orgs never test offboarding until a real termination exposes the gaps. You just proved yours works on day one.

human_layer.explanation: Correct path: identity first → role-based least-privilege access → hardened devices → human-layer controls logged → offboarding rehearsal. Onboarding isn't 'accounts created' — it's 'productive, secure, and auditable by lunch.'

laptops_first.text: It's 10 AM: three people with laptops they can't log into, and you're now creating accounts under time pressure — mistakes love hurry. The right order was:

choices.label: Identity first — restart the morning
choices.feedback: Dependencies order themselves: identity → access → device → human.

laptops_first.explanation: Onboarding has a dependency chain. Start at the root: identity.

paperwork.text: Paperwork done by 9:30, but accounts are still provisioning and laptops sit idle. Parallelize: technical chain first, paperwork alongside. Restart:

choices.label: Kick off account creation at 8:00 sharp
choices.feedback: Lead with the long pole — provisioning — and fill the wait with paperwork.

paperwork.explanation: Start the slowest step first. Everything else fills the gaps.

domain_admin.text: Week three: one 'temporary' Domain Admin account is used to 'fix' a GPO — badly — and the audit flags all three. 'Temporary' privilege is permanent risk. The policy:

choices.label: Least privilege from minute one; elevation via ticketed, time-bound process
choices.feedback: There's no safe amount of standing Domain Admin for a new hire.

domain_admin.explanation: Temporary elevated access is the most common privilege-creep vector in IT.

clone.text: Six months later nobody can explain why the hires have backup-operator rights on the finance server. Cloned access is unreviewed access. Use:

choices.label: The role-based access matrix
choices.feedback: Matrices get reviewed; clones get forgotten.

clone.explanation: Grant by role, not by copying a human.

ask_hire.text: The hires requested (and got) local admin 'for drivers' — now one has a crypto miner. Access decisions belong to:

choices.label: The access matrix and their manager, not the new hire
choices.feedback: Day-one hires can't assess their own risk footprint.

ask_hire.explanation: Access is granted by role definition, not self-service.

skip_brief.text: Month two: one of the three clicks a phishing link 'from IT.' The briefing you skipped was the control for exactly this. Everyone gets:

choices.label: The briefing on day one, logged
choices.feedback: Phishing doesn't check job titles.

skip_brief.explanation: Security awareness is per-human, not per-role.

later.text: 'Later this week' became never. The hires' first 72 hours — peak credential-theft risk — had no phishing briefing. Schedule it:

choices.label: Day one, before lunch
choices.feedback: The riskiest window gets the control first.

later.explanation: Controls delayed past the risk window are theater.

end.text: Scenario complete. Three hires productive, secure, and auditable by lunch — plus a tested offboarding process. That's onboarding done right.

choices.label: Next scenario
choices.feedback: Try the Domain Admin shortcut and watch month three.

end.explanation: Mastery = dependency-ordered provisioning + least privilege + human controls + provable offboarding.
